subjects.title: Structured discovery and the translation table
learn: Discovery is a three-step filter: listen to the business goal, translate it into requirements, assumptions and unresolved constraints, and write it down before the conversation moves on.

A stated preference ('seamless', 'easy', 'fast') hides a constraint; ask what would break the experience, what the user must never notice, what happens behind the scenes, and what must hold when something fails.
Four buckets: what the system must do, must NOT do, must cost, and must PROVE. Stakeholders rarely volunteer the must-not-do items.

A translation-table row holds: stakeholder statement as said, implied constraint, required architectural decision, and the assumption documented while unconfirmed. One row per item keeps the reasoning intact into design.

The expensive failure is an unstated constraint that surfaces at legal or compliance review. Finish the four-category question set before proposing anything; a confident sketch is the moment the questions stop.
traps: Recording the word: writing 'seamless' as the requirement captures the summary, not a testable, bounded constraint the design can be built against.
Sketching early: a plausible architecture makes the stakeholder assume you have the information, and the questions stop at exactly the wrong moment.
Review dismissal: treat every 'it's just a review' as a constraint to chase down; it may be a required architectural gate, not an optional convenience.
Over-assigning to Claude: the must-do bucket separates the work Claude owns from the work that stays with an existing system or a human.
Forgetting must-prove: proof obligations in regulated workflows are requirements and are far cheaper to find in discovery than in a legal review weeks later.

questions.stem: A stakeholder says the new assistant must 'feel seamless'. Which next move best reflects structured discovery?
options: Record 'seamless' as the requirement and move on to design so momentum is kept
Ask what would make the experience feel not seamless, to surface the hidden constraints
Commit to a sub-second latency target immediately and ask the stakeholder to sign off
Ask the stakeholder to rank the product features they care about most
questions.explanation: A stated preference sits on top of constraints. Asking what would make it feel not seamless exposes constraints such as a latency budget the user should not notice, an uninterrupted handoff and a failure state that hides system internals. Picking a latency number straight away guesses at one constraint and ignores the rest.
questions.mnemonic: Seamless is the label; 'what would break it?' opens the box.

questions.stem: In a kickoff, a claims director says the tool should be 'simple and intuitive' for adjusters. What is the best way to treat this statement?
options: Add 'simple and intuitive' to the requirements list verbatim, since the director owns the wording of the goal
Choose a single delivery route, because fewer platforms is what simple means in architectural terms
Defer the wording to the design review, where the UX team will define what simple should mean
Treat it as a signal: ask what would break it, what users must never notice, and failure behaviour
questions.explanation: Experience words like simple, easy, fast and intuitive signal that more discovery is needed. Ask what would break the experience, what the user must never notice and what happens when something fails. Writing the word down verbatim leaves the design inheriting your assumptions.
questions.mnemonic: Easy, fast, simple, seamless: each word is a question mark, not a requirement.

questions.stem: Which sequence describes the three-step filter a discovery conversation should function as?
options: Listen, sketch the architecture, then confirm the sketch with the stakeholder
Gather features, estimate cost, then present a recommended pattern
Listen to the goal, translate it into requirements and assumptions, then write it down
Write the requirements first, then listen for corrections, then translate for the design team
questions.explanation: Discovery is listen, translate, write down, and the write-down happens before the conversation moves on. Without it the design inherits the architect's assumptions. Sketching during the call replaces the translation step with a guess.
questions.mnemonic: Listen, translate, write down: ears, brain, paper.

questions.stem: Which TWO of the following are among the four question buckets used to turn a vague stakeholder statement into requirements? Select TWO.
options: What the system must prove
Which cloud vendor the stakeholder prefers
Which model tier the team enjoys most
What the system must not do
Which team will own the sales relationship
questions.explanation: The four buckets are must do, must not do, must cost and must prove. Vendor preference and sales ownership are not discovery buckets; a vendor preference may emerge from them but is not one of the four questions.
questions.mnemonic: Do, Don't, Dollars, Demonstrate: the four D-questions of discovery.

questions.stem: Which discovery bucket do stakeholders rarely volunteer, so the architect must ask for it explicitly?
options: What the system must do, expressed as business outcomes the stakeholder describes naturally
What the system must cost, expressed as a latency target or per-interaction ceiling
What the system must not do, including boundaries and cases that must route to a human
How the system will be hosted, expressed as a cloud preference for the program
questions.explanation: Boundaries, prohibited actions and human-routed cases are rarely volunteered, so they have to be asked for. Must-do capabilities are what stakeholders talk about naturally, so they surface unprompted.
questions.mnemonic: Nobody volunteers the 'don't': ask for the fence before the field.

questions.stem: After a call, an architect's notes list only capabilities the stakeholders want. What is the most significant gap in the discovery record?
options: No cost ceiling, since a per-interaction budget is always set later by finance teams
No explicit prohibited actions or human-routed cases, because nobody was asked for them
No preferred model name, which blocks the design from starting in the next sprint
No ranking of requested features by how many users asked for each of them
questions.explanation: Stakeholders describe what they want and seldom the boundaries, so a capabilities-only record signals the must-not-do bucket was never asked. Cost is also a bucket, but the gap named here is the one that stakeholders almost never fill on their own.
questions.mnemonic: Capabilities-only notes mean the fence questions were never asked.

questions.stem: Why does the discovery translation table hold exactly one row per discovery item?
options: It keeps each item's reasoning intact from discovery into design and keeps assumptions visible
It keeps the table short enough for an executive sponsor to approve in one sitting
It lets each row be assigned to a separate delivery team as a work package
It lets the table replace the production-signal governance table after launch
questions.explanation: Each discovery item becomes one row capturing the statement as said, the implied constraint, the decision it forces and any assumption. One row per item keeps the reasoning intact as the work moves into design and keeps assumptions top of mind. The governance table is a separate artifact for the live deployment.
questions.mnemonic: One item, one row: the reasoning travels intact from discovery into design.

questions.stem: A sponsor wants discovery cut to one short call so the team can start building sooner. What is the architect's best response?
options: Agree, because hidden constraints are cheaper to find and fix during the build itself
Agree, because the legal and compliance review will supply any requirements still missing
Agree, because a quick prototype will reveal every constraint the stakeholder forgot to mention
Push back: finding the real constraints now costs far less than redesigning after compliance review
questions.explanation: A discovery call that runs long enough to identify the real constraints is far cheaper than redesigning after a hidden constraint emerges in legal or compliance review. Relying on the build or the compliance review to surface constraints is how they become production blockers, when change costs most.
questions.mnemonic: A longer call is cheap; a late redesign is not.

questions.stem: Which outcome should an architect leave a discovery call with?
options: An agreed architecture sketch the stakeholder has already approved in the room
A firm prototype date that keeps the stakeholder's momentum going after the call
A record of the constraints hidden in the business description that the design can follow
A ranked list of the product features the stakeholder mentioned most often during the call
questions.explanation: Discovery reveals whether you are solving the right problem: listen to what the business is trying to achieve, identify the constraints hidden in that description, and leave with a record the design can follow. An approved sketch on the call is the moment the questions stop, not the goal of the call.
questions.mnemonic: Leave discovery with a record, not a rendering.

questions.stem: Which description best captures the expensive failure mode of weak discovery?
options: A discovery call that runs long enough to uncover the real constraints early
A translation table with so many rows that the design team cannot read it
An assumption labelled as an assumption that is later confirmed by the owner
An unstated constraint that survives until legal or compliance review, when change costs most
questions.explanation: The costly failure is the constraint nobody stated that appears at the production review blocker stage, when changing course is slowest and most expensive. A longer discovery call is the cheaper alternative, not the failure.
questions.mnemonic: Hidden constraints grow pricier every week they stay hidden.

questions.stem: Six weeks into a build, compliance demands an audit trail the design never included. Which discovery question would most directly have caught this earlier?
options: What must the system prove, and to whom, in a regulated workflow?
What must the system cost, stated as a per-interaction ceiling or volume forecast?
What must the system do, stated as business outcomes rather than product features?
What would make the experience feel not seamless to the end user?
questions.explanation: Proof obligations belong in the must-prove bucket, and finding them in discovery is far cheaper than in a legal review weeks later. The cost and must-do questions would not reveal an evidence requirement.
questions.mnemonic: Must-prove asked early beats must-prove demanded late.

questions.stem: An architect is running discovery for a consumer lending workflow. When should the evidence the deployment must produce for regulators be identified?
options: After the pilot proves business value, so effort is not spent on a use case that may be dropped
At the first external audit, when the regulator states exactly which evidence it expects to see
When the outcome document is written at close, since that is where controls are first recorded
During discovery, as part of the requirement set, because a later legal review costs far more
questions.explanation: What the system must prove is part of the requirement set in regulated workflows, so proof obligations are identified in discovery; finding them in a legal review weeks later is far more expensive. Waiting for the pilot or an audit lets the missing evidence become a production blocker.
questions.mnemonic: Regulated? Ask 'what must we prove?' on day one, not in legal review.

questions.stem: In the discovery filter, the second step translates the stakeholder's business goal into which THREE things? Select THREE.
options: Requirements the design must support
An architecture sketch ready for stakeholder sign-off
Assumptions that still need confirmation
A shortlist of candidate delivery routes
Unresolved constraints that could block the solution
questions.explanation: Translation turns the stated goal into requirements, assumptions and unresolved constraints, showing what the design must support, what still needs confirmation and what could block the solution later. A sketch or a route shortlist is design work, and starting it mid-call is what stops the questions.
questions.mnemonic: Translate into three: must support, must confirm, might block.

questions.stem: During discovery, a stakeholder gives a three-second p95 response target, a ceiling of two cents per interaction and a forecast of 80,000 calls a month. Which discovery bucket do these answers belong in?
options: What the system must prove, as evidence obligations for later review
What the system must cost, as budget constraints the stakeholder controls
What the system must not do, as boundaries and prohibited actions
What the system must do, as capabilities the deployment delivers
questions.explanation: The must-cost bucket holds the budget constraint expressed in terms the stakeholder controls, which includes a latency target, a per-interaction cost ceiling and a volume forecast. Must-do is tempting because the volume describes usage, but must-do captures capabilities as business outcomes, not budgets.
questions.mnemonic: Cost bucket holds the clock, the cents and the count: latency, ceiling, volume.

questions.stem: An architect fills the 'must do' discovery bucket with features such as 'summarize button' and 'auto-tagging'. What should this bucket capture instead?
options: The per-interaction cost ceiling and volume forecast that bound each capability
The prohibited actions and cases that must be routed to a human reviewer
The evidence artifacts the deployment must produce for a later legal review
Capabilities stated as business outcomes, separating Claude's work from systems and humans
questions.explanation: Must-do captures the capabilities the deployment must deliver, expressed as business outcomes rather than features, and is where Claude's work is separated from work that stays with an existing system or a human. The cost ceiling and volume forecast belong in the must-cost bucket.
questions.mnemonic: Must-do speaks outcomes, not buttons.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about the four discovery buckets are correct? Select TWO.
options: The must-prove bucket can wait for legal review, since evidence is a later concern
The must-do bucket states capabilities as business outcomes rather than features
The must-not-do bucket is usually volunteered by stakeholders without prompting
The must-cost bucket includes latency targets and volume forecasts as well as cost ceilings
The must-cost bucket is expressed in token counts the engineering team controls
questions.explanation: Must-do is expressed as business outcomes, and must-cost covers latency targets, per-interaction cost ceilings and volume forecasts in terms the stakeholder controls. Must-prove obligations are far cheaper to find in discovery than in a later legal review, and must-not-do items are rarely volunteered.
questions.mnemonic: Do = outcomes; Cost = clock, cents, count, in the stakeholder's terms.

questions.stem: After a discovery call, which TWO items in the record are ready for the design to be built against? Select TWO.
options: The stakeholder's word 'seamless', recorded exactly as it was said
A p95 response-time target the stakeholder confirmed in follow-up questions
A ranked wish list of features gathered from several user interviews
A per-interaction cost ceiling stated in terms the stakeholder controls
The architect's preferred integration pattern from a previous engagement
questions.explanation: A testable, bounded constraint is what the design can be built against, and a confirmed p95 target and a cost ceiling both qualify. A preference word recorded verbatim only tells you where to investigate, and a wish list or a favourite pattern is not a constraint at all.
questions.mnemonic: Preferences point the way; bounded, testable constraints are what you build against.

questions.stem: A stakeholder says the new tool must be 'fast and easy'. Which THREE follow-up questions help turn this into design constraints? Select THREE.
options: Which model tier is the newest one we could use today?
What would break that experience for the user?
What must the user never notice happening?
Which features do competitors already ship?
What must still be true when something goes wrong?
questions.explanation: Experience words such as fast, easy, seamless, simple and intuitive signal that more discovery is needed. Ask what would break the experience, what the user must never notice, what has to happen behind the scenes and what must still be true when something goes wrong. Model tiers and competitor features do not surface the constraint.
questions.mnemonic: Break it, hide it, fail it: three questions under every experience word.

questions.stem: Which set of columns makes up each row of the discovery translation table?
options: Requirement, capability list, architecture sketch, boundary conditions, and the statement of work
Options considered, criteria weighed, the recommendation, and the risks that remain afterwards
Stakeholder statement as said, implied constraint, required architectural decision, and the assumption documented
Signal type, review trigger, architect action, and the regulated-industry checkpoint for it
questions.explanation: Each discovery item becomes one row holding the statement as it was said, the constraint it implies, the architectural decision that constraint forces, and any assumption documented while the constraint is unconfirmed. The other options describe the scoping sequence, the decision package and the governance table.
questions.mnemonic: Said, implied, decided, assumed: four columns per row.

questions.stem: A stakeholder says all users sit in one country, but nobody has confirmed this with the data owner. How should the discovery record handle the statement?
options: Record it as a row with its decision, and label the assumption explicitly for confirmation
Leave it out of the record until the data owner confirms it, so nothing unverified enters
Write it into the record as a settled fact, since the stakeholder knows their own user base
Defer it to the compliance review, where the data owner will be asked to settle the point
questions.explanation: Each discovery item becomes a row, and when its constraint is not yet confirmed the row documents the assumption so it stays visible until confirmed. Leaving the item out loses it; writing it as a settled fact hides an assumption, which is how the design inherits unverified beliefs.
questions.mnemonic: Unconfirmed goes in the row, labelled 'assumption: confirm', never as fact.

questions.stem: Partway through a discovery call, an architect sketches a confident design and the stakeholder happily agrees. Why is this moment dangerous?
options: Stakeholders tend to reject sketches early, so momentum is lost before requirements are set
A sketch locks in a model tier before eval data exists, which raises later running costs
A plausible sketch signals the architect already has the information needed, so the questions stop
The stakeholder may confuse the sketch with a finished design and expect a working prototype immediately
questions.explanation: Plausibility is what makes it dangerous: a stakeholder who hears a confident architecture assumes the architect has the information to build it, so the questions that would surface hidden constraints never get asked. The problem is not rejection.
questions.mnemonic: A pretty sketch stops the questions.

questions.stem: Which practice best protects a discovery call from turning into a premature design session?
options: Propose a design early so the stakeholder can react, then collect missing constraints during the build
Keep the call short and leave constraint gathering to the legal and compliance review that follows
Agree a prototype date on the call, then add review steps once the stakeholder sees the output
Finish the four-category question set before proposing anything, and chase every 'just a review' as a constraint
questions.explanation: The protective move is deliberately boring: complete the four question categories before proposing any design, and treat every 'it's just a review' as a constraint to chase down. Deferring constraints to the build or to compliance review is exactly how hidden constraints become expensive blockers.
questions.mnemonic: Four buckets full before one box is drawn.

questions.stem: Why should items surfaced in a discovery call be written down before the conversation moves on?
options: So the stakeholder can sign a statement of work before the call has ended
Because written notes are needed only later, for the project's billing records
So the call can be shortened, since written items need no further questions
Without the record, the design inherits the architect's assumptions and mismatches surface late
questions.explanation: The design needs a clear record to follow. Without the write-down step, the design inherits the architect's assumptions, and the mismatch may only appear much later, when changing trajectory is slower, harder and more expensive. A shorter call is not the point; capturing what was heard is.
questions.mnemonic: Unwritten discovery becomes the architect's guesswork, found out late.

subjects.title: Communicating trade-offs
learn: The architect's job is to make decisions possible, not to resolve the trade-off in advance; present a package of options, criteria, recommendation and remaining risks.

Decision frame: what do we gain, what do we give up, what happens if we choose now and must reverse later, and (regulated) what it does to compliance posture. Reversal cost is the one most often skipped.
Description competency for stakeholders: lead with the business outcome, frame limitations honestly, and anticipate the peer-proof demand so the stakeholder can justify the choice to others.
Trade-off map examples: large context vs retrieval (evaluate prompt caching for static content), logging detail vs latency (compliance gap), single route vs multi-platform (blocked cutover).
False alignment: a decision looks approved in the room but reversal cost was never made explicit; name the reversal cost especially when the design feels obviously simpler.
traps: Pre-resolved verdicts: presenting only the conclusion looks decisive but leaves the stakeholder approving something without understanding what came with it.
Answering only what was asked: an accurate technical answer can still miss the approver's real question, what happens to the business if the choice is wrong and must be reversed.
Treating per-call cost as fixed: for static documents held in context, evaluate prompt caching before accepting the cost as given.
Technical precision as sufficiency: an accurate recommendation can still be unusable if the approver cannot translate it into business consequence.
Room agreement as proof: a yes at the end of a complete presentation can still be false alignment.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the architect's role when presenting a significant design trade-off to a stakeholder?
options: Resolve the trade-off before the meeting and present the single best technical answer
Describe the options clearly enough that the stakeholder can make an informed choice
Present as many options as possible without a recommendation to stay neutral
Hold back the downsides until the stakeholder has agreed to the direction
questions.explanation: The job is to make decisions possible, which means describing options clearly enough for an informed choice. Presenting only the conclusion makes the decision look clear but weak.
questions.mnemonic: Don't hand down a verdict; hand over a decision.

questions.stem: An architect arrives with a single recommended design and a polished justification, and no alternatives. Why is this approach weak?
options: The recommendation may be technically wrong, and stakeholders prefer an unfinished proposal to a polished one
Executives dislike recommendations, so they should always be left to the stakeholders to form themselves
If the downside appears later, the stakeholder feels they approved a recommendation without understanding its price
A single design cannot be documented using a translation table or a decision record afterwards
questions.explanation: Presenting only the conclusion hides the trade-off, so when the downside shows up the stakeholder feels they did not make an informed choice. A recommendation is still wanted, but inside a package that includes options, criteria and risks.
questions.mnemonic: A verdict without its price tag becomes a grievance later.

questions.stem: Which THREE questions belong to the simple decision frame for presenting a trade-off? Select THREE.
options: What do we gain?
Which engineer on the team will implement it?
What happens if we choose this now but have to reverse it later?
In regulated environments, what does this do to our compliance posture?
Which competitor has already chosen the same option?
questions.explanation: The frame asks what we gain, what we give up, what happens if we must reverse later, and the compliance impact in regulated environments. Who implements it and what competitors did are not part of the frame.
questions.mnemonic: Gain, give up, go back, guard compliance: four G-questions.

questions.stem: Of the decision-frame questions, which is the one most often skipped, and often the one that changes the meeting?
options: What do we gain from the option, in the stakeholder's own goal terms?
What do we give up by choosing it, in cost, latency or risk?
What is the vendor's roadmap for features over the next year?
What happens if we choose this now but have to reverse it later?
questions.explanation: The reversal question is skipped most often, and it shifts the discussion from the better technical answer to the better business choice. Gains and give-ups are the questions people usually remember to answer.
questions.mnemonic: The skipped question is the cost of going back.

questions.stem: A review covers what a design gains and what it gives up, and the room feels aligned. Which element is still missing before the approval is truly informed?
options: The cost to the business of reversing the choice once the system depends on it
A detailed diagram of every component in the production route and its dependencies
A comparison of the prompt styles used in the pilot and their eval scores
The list of engineers who attended the design sessions and their responsibilities
questions.explanation: Reversal cost is the third element of the frame, and without it the approver cannot judge what a wrong choice would cost later. A diagram or attendee list does not address the consequence of reversing a decision.
questions.mnemonic: Gain and give-up are half a decision; reversal cost completes it.

questions.stem: Which set of contents makes up the decision package presented to a stakeholder?
options: Options considered, criteria weighed, a recommendation, and the risks that remain
A recommendation, a diagram, a delivery date, and a cost estimate
Options considered, a vendor comparison, a demo script, and a budget
A recommendation, a rejected alternative, a test plan, and an owner
questions.explanation: The package is options, criteria, recommendation and remaining risks, so the stakeholder accepts a decision they can defend to their own leadership. The other lists omit criteria or remaining risks.
questions.mnemonic: Options, criteria, recommendation, risks: the package, not the verdict.

questions.stem: Which TWO practices belong to applying the Description competency when communicating with stakeholders? Select TWO.
options: Lead with the architecture so the stakeholder sees the engineering depth
Frame the system's limitations honestly, since clearly stated limits build trust
Remove limitations from the summary to keep the message positive
Lead with the business outcome rather than the architecture
Use the same technical vocabulary for every audience to stay precise
questions.explanation: Description means leading with the business outcome and framing limitations honestly, matched to the audience's AI familiarity without losing accuracy. Hiding limits or leading with architecture works against stakeholder trust and understanding.
questions.mnemonic: Outcome first, limits honest, justification in hand.

questions.stem: A security director will need to justify the chosen design to the leadership team afterwards. What should the architect ensure at the end of the conversation?
options: The director has approved the design verbally in the room
The director leaves with the justification they can use with their own peers
The director has seen the full list of model parameters used
The director has deferred the justification to the architect for later meetings
questions.explanation: Anticipating the peer-proof demand means the stakeholder leaves with the justification needed to defend the choice to others. A verbal yes without usable justification risks the approval later being withdrawn.
questions.mnemonic: Approval travels only if the justification travels with it.

questions.stem: A design keeps a static policy document in the prompt on every call instead of building retrieval. What should the architect state about per-call cost?
options: It is fixed by the model tier, so only building a retrieval layer can lower it
It will drop automatically as production volume grows, so no action is needed
It becomes irrelevant once the full document stays in view on every call
Prompt caching can recover much of the input cost on static content, so evaluate it first
questions.explanation: Larger context gains simplicity but gives up per-call cost and speed at scale, and caching static content can recover much of the input cost. Treating per-call cost as fixed ignores that lever.
questions.mnemonic: Static document in context? Check caching before blaming cost.

questions.stem: A team proposes reducing logging detail to gain faster responses in a regulated workload. What does the trade-off map say a wrong, reversed choice could cost?
options: A slower response that users will tolerate
A potential compliance gap requiring remediation
A larger prompt cache that raises storage cost
A change of model tier at the next renewal
questions.explanation: Less logging buys speed but reduces visibility into each interaction, and in a regulated workload that can create a compliance gap needing remediation. The other options are not the stated consequence.
questions.mnemonic: Trim the logs for speed, and compliance sends the bill.

questions.stem: A team picks one delivery route for lower build complexity. Which reversal cost should the architect name for the stakeholder?
options: Higher authentication complexity across several different logging profiles in production
A loss of the one consistent logging profile that the single route provided
A delayed or blocked cutover if the route cannot meet a late residency requirement
A permanent ban on adding another platform once the first route is live
questions.explanation: A single route gains simplicity and one consistent auth and logging profile, but gives up flexibility; the reversal cost is a delayed or blocked cutover when a residency or deployment need appears late. Added complexity is what the multi-platform option costs instead.
questions.mnemonic: One road is simple until residency closes it.

questions.stem: What is 'false alignment' in a tradeoff presentation?
options: A decision looks approved in the room, but reversal cost was never made explicit
Two stakeholders approve different options during the same meeting without noticing the conflict
An architect presents an option that the delivery team has not yet built or tested
A stakeholder rejects the recommendation in the room but still approves the budget
questions.explanation: False alignment is an apparent yes where the reversal cost was never named, so the real consequence only appears after commitment. Disagreement among stakeholders is a different problem.
questions.mnemonic: A yes in the room can still be a no on the invoice.

questions.stem: On the tradeoff translation map, a team chooses a larger context window per call over retrieval. Which TWO costs does the map list if this choice proves wrong and must be reversed? Select TWO.
options: Reworking the architecture after cost spikes in production
A compliance gap from reduced logging that needs remediation
A blocked cutover when a late residency requirement appears
The credibility hit of explaining an avoidable expense surprise
Losing the full document in view on every single call
questions.explanation: For larger context over retrieval, the reversal cost is reworking the architecture after cost spikes in production plus the credibility hit of an avoidable expense surprise. A compliance gap belongs to the logging-versus-latency row, and a blocked cutover to the single-route row.
questions.mnemonic: Big context reversed: rebuild after the spike, and own the surprise.

questions.stem: When is it most important for an architect to name the reversal cost explicitly in a tradeoff presentation?
options: Only when the stakeholder asks a direct question about cost
When the recommended design feels like the obviously simpler choice
Only when the workload sits in a regulated environment
Only after the first production invoice has been received
questions.explanation: Name all three elements every time, and name the reversal cost especially when the design feels obviously simpler, because an approval given without understanding reversal cost is not an informed choice. Waiting for a cost question or an invoice is how false alignment forms.
questions.mnemonic: The simpler it looks, the louder you name the cost of going back.

subjects.title: Feedback loops and SLAs
learn: Live deployments drift: quality erodes gradually rather than breaking dramatically, and teams without a feedback loop may not notice until users feel it.
The feedback loop is a decision layer above observability: Signals, Triage, Decide, Act, Review. Decide chooses between team fix, stakeholder review or no action.

An SLA names what is measured, what counts as a breach, and what happens on breach. Thresholds trace to tangible sources: latency to UX expectation, availability to business criticality, quality to eval results and acceptance criteria.

Cost is the expectation that breaks most after launch: production volume often runs one to two orders of magnitude above pilot; give a forecast, name spend controls (caching, model tiering, budget alerts) before the first invoice.
Regulated deployments add scheduled review checkpoints independent of incidents; a governance table maps signal to trigger, architect action and regulated checkpoint.
traps: Dashboards equal feedback: observability collects signals, but without a rule mapping signal to trigger and owner, a slow drift stays invisible.
Hard-failure alerting only: a slow quality drift may never cross an error threshold, so the governance table must map slow drifts as well as hard failures to triggers.
Arbitrary thresholds: a number that cannot be tied to UX expectation, business criticality or eval results is just a target someone chose.
Cost shock: pilot cost looks trivial; production volume turns it into a five-figure monthly line unless forecast and controls were framed first.
Incident-only reviews: regulated checkpoints must run on a schedule even when nothing has gone wrong.

questions.stem: An internal policy Q&A tool has been live for a year with no feedback loop. Which pattern of degradation should the architect expect?
options: A single dramatic outage that alerts the whole team at once
A sudden quality drop on the day a model update is released
Quality that holds steady until the first quarterly review
Gradual erosion of quality that may go unseen until users feel it
questions.explanation: Drift is hard to catch because nothing breaks dramatically: quality erodes gradually, and a team without a feedback loop may not see the decline until users already feel it. A single outage or a sudden drop would be noticed; the slow slide is what goes unseen.
questions.mnemonic: Drift is a slow leak, not a burst pipe.

questions.stem: How does the feedback loop relate to the observability stack?
options: It replaces the stack by producing its own latency and error metrics
It is a decision layer above the stack that turns signals into triage, decisions and actions
It is a reporting tool that formats the stack's output for quarterly review
It is a sub-feature of the stack that raises alerts when thresholds are crossed
questions.explanation: Observability supplies the raw signals; the feedback loop decides which need attention, who acts and what changes. It is not another metrics source or a formatting step.
questions.mnemonic: Observability measures; the feedback loop decides.

questions.stem: Which is the correct order of the feedback loop's five stages?
options: Signals, Decide, Triage, Act, Review
Triage, Signals, Decide, Review, Act
Signals, Triage, Decide, Act, Review
Signals, Triage, Act, Decide, Review
questions.explanation: The loop runs Signals, Triage, Decide, Act, Review, where Review checks whether the response worked and whether the rule needs to change. Acting before deciding skips the judgement step.
questions.mnemonic: STDAR: Signals, Triage, Decide, Act, Review.

questions.stem: Which THREE things must an SLA make clear? Select THREE.
options: What is being measured
Which cloud region hosts the monitoring tools
What counts as a breach
What happens when a breach occurs
Which engineer wrote the first prompt
questions.explanation: An SLA names the measure, the breach definition and the consequence of a breach. Hosting region and prompt authorship are not part of the SLA definition.
questions.mnemonic: Measure, breach, consequence: the SLA triangle.

questions.stem: Where should a latency threshold in an SLA come from?
options: The best p95 the team achieved during load testing
The default value suggested by the monitoring tool
The latency of the previous system, regardless of user needs
The user experience expectation identified earlier in discovery
questions.explanation: Latency thresholds should reflect the UX expectation set earlier, which keeps the SLA defensible. A number chosen because it was achievable or because it was a default has no tangible source.
questions.mnemonic: Latency limit comes from what users expect, not what tools suggest.

questions.stem: An architect must set availability and quality thresholds for a claims deployment. Which pairing of source to threshold is correct?
options: Availability from business criticality; quality from eval results and acceptance criteria
Availability from the cloud provider's published figure; quality from user complaints
Availability from the pilot's uptime; quality from the cost budget
Availability from the UX expectation; quality from business criticality
questions.explanation: Availability reflects how critical the deployment is to the business, and quality reflects the eval results and acceptance criteria already established. Mixing the sources breaks the traceability that keeps an SLA defensible.
questions.mnemonic: Uptime follows criticality; quality follows the evals.

questions.stem: A proposed SLA sets a 98% quality target, but nobody can say where the figure came from. What is the most accurate assessment?
options: It is acceptable because round numbers are easier to communicate
It is probably just a target someone chose because it sounded reasonable
It is acceptable if the monitoring tool can measure it
It should be raised to match the best result in testing
questions.explanation: If a threshold cannot be tied to a tangible source such as eval results or acceptance criteria, it is probably an arbitrary target. Measurability does not make it defensible.
questions.mnemonic: No source, no SLA: an untraceable number is a guess.

questions.stem: Which expectation most often breaks after launch, and why?
options: Latency, because networks slow down noticeably once the full user base is onboarded
Cost, because production volume often runs one to two orders of magnitude above pilot
Availability, because cloud providers change their commitments soon after a launch
Quality, because the eval suite is retired once the pilot has ended
questions.explanation: Cost is the expectation that breaks most; a trivial pilot cost can become a five-figure monthly line at production volume. The other expectations can degrade, but cost is the one that breaks most often after launch.
questions.mnemonic: Pilot pennies, production pounds: one to two orders of magnitude.

questions.stem: To pre-empt the cost surprise after launch, which TWO actions should the architect take before the first invoice? Select TWO.
options: Provide a consumption forecast at expected production volume
Wait for the first invoice, then explain the model-tiering narrative
Name the spend-control posture such as caching, model tiering and budget alerts
Quote only the pilot's per-call cost to keep the message simple
Raise the SLA latency threshold to reduce spend
questions.explanation: Give a forecast at production volume and state the spend-control posture, framing model tiering before the first invoice rather than after it. Quoting only pilot cost or waiting for the invoice reproduces the surprise.
questions.mnemonic: Forecast first, controls named, narrative before the invoice.

questions.stem: How do regulated deployments differ in feedback-loop design?
options: They only review output when an incident or a complaint has been reported
They replace SLAs entirely with thresholds supplied directly by the regulator
They add scheduled review checkpoints that run even when nothing has gone wrong
They skip triage because every signal in a regulated system must be escalated
questions.explanation: Some reviews, such as periodic output audits or residency confirmations, must happen on a defined schedule regardless of incidents. They are design-time obligations, not tasks to add later.
questions.mnemonic: Regulated means the calendar triggers the review, not the alarm.

questions.stem: In the governance table, an output quality score crosses the threshold drawn from the eval suite. What is the architect's action?
options: Diagnose prompt, data or model drift, then decide whether to iterate or re-architect
Raise the threshold to match the new score and continue operating as normal
Escalate straight to the regulator and trigger a periodic output audit immediately
Switch to a cheaper model tier in order to restore the previous score
questions.explanation: The architect diagnoses prompt, data or model drift and decides whether to iterate or re-architect. The regulated audit runs on its own schedule regardless of score.
questions.mnemonic: Score drops: prompt, data or model? Diagnose, then iterate or rebuild.

questions.stem: Observability shows a one-off latency spike, a sustained eval-score decline and an intermittent tool error. Why can't the team simply act on each signal as it arrives?
options: Each signal needs the vendor's approval before any corrective change can be made
Only error-rate signals are actionable, so the remaining signals should be ignored
A signal is not a decision: some are noise, others matter only if they recur
Every signal must first be escalated straight to the business stakeholder for review
questions.explanation: Observability supplies raw material such as latency, error rates and eval scores, but a signal by itself is not yet a decision: one spike may be noise, another may point to a real problem, and a third may matter only if it keeps happening. The feedback loop is the decision layer that triages them.
questions.mnemonic: Signals are raw material; the loop turns them into decisions.

questions.stem: A team has live dashboards and configured alerts and concludes that stakeholder feedback is therefore covered. What is missing to make this a feedback loop?
options: More latency percentiles and detailed error breakdowns added to the existing dashboards
A lower error-rate threshold, so that the existing alerts fire earlier than now
A longer launch review attended by the full stakeholder group and the vendor
A governance table mapping every signal, slow drifts included, to trigger, action and owner
questions.explanation: A dashboard collects and displays signals; a feedback loop maps each signal to a trigger, an owner and a required action, covering slow drifts as well as hard failures. A slow drift may never cross an error threshold, so tighter alerts or more charts still leave it with no trigger.
questions.mnemonic: Table, not dashboard: signal, trigger, action, owner.

questions.stem: In the governance table, what is the review trigger for the data-residency configuration signal?
options: A cost-per-interaction budget breach that exceeds the envelope agreed in discovery
A latency p95 crossing the user-experience budget set during design
A drop in the eval score below the threshold drawn from the eval suite
Scheduled confirmation, with posture recorded and any drift flagged immediately
questions.explanation: Residency is checked on a scheduled confirmation, with the posture recorded and any drift flagged immediately. The other triggers belong to cost, latency and quality signals.
questions.mnemonic: Residency is checked on the calendar, not after the breach.

questions.stem: In the feedback loop, which stage determines whether an issue needs a team fix, a stakeholder review or no action?
options: Triage
Act
Decide
Review
questions.explanation: Decide chooses among a team fix, a stakeholder review or no action. Triage comes earlier and only sorts what needs attention now from what can wait; Act then carries out the correction, guardrail update or escalation.
questions.mnemonic: Triage sorts, Decide chooses who, Act does, Review checks the rule.

questions.stem: Which TWO pairings of feedback-loop stage and the question it answers are correct? Select TWO.
options: Signals: does the issue need a team fix or a stakeholder review?
Triage: what needs attention now, and what can wait?
Act: what is the system showing us across its dashboards?
Review: did the response work, and does the rule need to change?
Decide: which guardrail update has already been deployed?
questions.explanation: Triage separates what needs attention now from what can wait, and Review asks whether the response worked and whether the rule itself needs to change. Signals asks what the system is showing; Decide chooses between a team fix, a stakeholder review or no action.
questions.mnemonic: Review closes the loop by questioning the rule, not just the fix.

questions.stem: Latency p95 crosses the budget set from user-experience requirements. Investigation shows the system is well tuned and the budget itself was unrealistic. What does the governance table direct?
options: Re-architect the deployment until it meets the original p95 budget
Escalate to a stakeholder review, since the budget itself is wrong
Raise the p95 budget quietly so the alert stops firing every week
Trigger a periodic output audit against the documentation standard
questions.explanation: The latency row says investigate the bottleneck, then tune, or escalate to a stakeholder review if the budget itself is wrong. The budget came from user-experience requirements the stakeholder owns, so quietly changing it or re-architecting to an unrealistic number bypasses that decision.
questions.mnemonic: Wrong budget? Not your number to move: take it back to the stakeholder.

questions.stem: Cost per interaction crosses the budget envelope agreed in discovery. What is the architect's action according to the production-signal governance table?
options: Switch every call to the cheapest model tier at once, then report the saving to the stakeholder
Treat it as a regulated checkpoint and run a residency confirmation before any other change
Identify the driver, then bring a tradeoff to the stakeholder if the budget needs revisiting
Wait for the quarterly review, since cost is not a quality signal and rarely needs attention
questions.explanation: The cost row says identify the driver, then bring a tradeoff to the stakeholder if the budget envelope needs revisiting. Cutting every call to the cheapest tier skips both diagnosis and the stakeholder decision, and cost usually carries no regulated checkpoint.
questions.mnemonic: Cost over the envelope: find the driver, then table a tradeoff.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about the production-signal governance table are correct? Select TWO.
options: Latency p95 always carries a regulated checkpoint, whatever the logging setup
The cost trigger is a budget chosen after launch from observed spend
Regulated output quality gets a periodic audit on schedule, regardless of the eval score
Data residency is reviewed only when an alert fires on configuration drift
The latency trigger is the budget set from user-experience requirements
questions.explanation: The regulated checkpoint for output quality is a periodic audit against the documentation standard on a set schedule, regardless of score, and the latency trigger is the budget drawn from user-experience requirements. Latency usually has no regulated checkpoint unless it masks a logging gap, and residency is confirmed on a schedule, not on alert.
questions.mnemonic: Audits run on the calendar, not on the score.

questions.stem: Which part of running a feedback loop can observability tooling NOT do for the architect?
options: Collect latency, error-rate and usage metrics from the live system
Display eval scores and trends on shared team dashboards
Fire an alert when a configured threshold has been crossed
Judge which signals deserve attention and which are just noise
questions.explanation: The hardest part of the loop is deciding which signals deserve attention and which are noise, because observability tooling cannot make that judgment. Collecting metrics, displaying them and firing threshold alerts are exactly what the tooling already does.
questions.mnemonic: Tools collect and alert; only judgment separates signal from noise.

questions.stem: A sponsor questions the ongoing Architect time a feedback loop needs after launch. Which justification is strongest?
options: It removes the need to run an observability stack in production at all
It costs less than discovering decline at a quarterly review after every dashboard looked good
It is a one-off setup cost that ends once the governance table is written
Regulators require a fixed weekly hours budget for every live AI deployment
questions.explanation: The loop does create ongoing Architect effort, but that is cheaper than discovering decline in a quarterly review after every dashboard looked good. It sits on top of observability rather than replacing it, and it is ongoing work, not a one-off setup.
questions.mnemonic: Pay a little every week, or pay a lot at the quarterly review.

questions.stem: A healthcare deployment's documentation obligation requires periodic output audits. The team plans to set them up 'once the system is stable'. What is wrong with this plan?
options: Periodic audits are only needed after an eval score crosses its threshold, so none are due yet
Scheduled checkpoints are design-time obligations; built late they cost far more once proof is requested
Output audits belong to the compliance team, so the architect has no role in scheduling them
Stability is the right trigger, since audits during early drift would only measure launch noise
questions.explanation: Regulated review checkpoints run on a schedule even when nothing has gone wrong, and they are design-time obligations; if not built early they become far more expensive to establish when someone asks for proof. Tying audits to an eval threshold misses that they run regardless of score.
questions.mnemonic: Checkpoints are built in, not bolted on.

questions.stem: When should the production-signal governance table, mapping each signal to its trigger, action and regulatory checkpoint, exist?
options: After the first quarterly review, once real signals show which ones matter
After the first SLA breach, so triggers reflect a failure that really occurred
During handoff, so the inheriting engineer can tailor it to their own routine
Before launch, as the mechanism that turns policy into an operating routine
questions.explanation: The governance table should exist before launch; it is the mechanism that turns policy into an operating routine. Waiting for a quarterly review or a breach leaves slow drifts with no trigger, so signals exist but nothing decides they matter.
questions.mnemonic: Table before takeoff: policy becomes routine on day one.

questions.stem: When designing a feedback loop for a regulated deployment, which failure mode carries the biggest risk?
options: An alert threshold set too tightly, so the team is flooded with noise from minor spikes
A compliance checkpoint never wired to a trigger, so a standard violation runs for weeks
A dashboard showing too many signals, so stakeholders stop reading the weekly reports
A latency budget set from the pilot, so production traffic breaches it on launch day
questions.explanation: The biggest failure mode is a compliance checkpoint that was never wired to a trigger, letting a documented-standard violation run for weeks before a routine review catches it. Noisy alerts are a real complexity cost, but deciding signal versus noise is the hard part, not the biggest risk.
questions.mnemonic: An unwired checkpoint is a silent alarm.

subjects.title: Documentation for handoff and audit
learn: One document serves three readers: the inheriting engineer, the auditor, and the returning architect. Serving only one makes it incomplete.

Handoff recipients need rejected alternatives and the rationale for each rejection; compliance reviewers need obligation, control, owner and evidence artifact (the control register carried forward), not assertions.
Returning architects need dated decisions, assumptions labelled as assumptions, and open items with owners and resolution criteria.
Completeness test: can a competent architect who was not in the room make a safe change after reading it?

Checklist fields: decision, rejected alternatives, tradeoff named, owner, evidence artifact, audit-ready status. Documentation is the handoff stage; the feedback loop is the monitoring-and-iteration stage.
traps: Recording what, not why: a design without its rationale cannot be safely changed, so a successor may reverse a load-bearing decision and reintroduce a constraint violation.
Assertions as evidence: a statement that a control exists is not enough; the reviewer needs an evidence artifact showing it operating.
Assumptions as facts: embedding assumptions in the text as settled facts leaves the returning architect unable to tell what was confirmed.
Right decision, wrong reason: without rejected alternatives, a successor reverses the right decision for the wrong reason or defends the wrong one.
Writing it later: rationale not recorded at design time leaves with the architect and is reconstructed from email threads, if at all.

questions.stem: Which THREE readers must architecture documentation serve to be considered complete? Select THREE.
options: The inheriting engineer who had no part in the build
The end user who submits requests to the system
The auditor looking for evidence that a control is operating
The returning architect who has lost the design context
The vendor's account executive preparing a renewal
questions.explanation: The three readers are the inheriting engineer, the auditor and the returning architect. A document built for only one of them is incomplete even when detailed.
questions.mnemonic: Inheritor, auditor, returner: three readers, one document.

questions.stem: A handoff document is highly detailed for the engineer taking over but has no control evidence and no dated decisions. How should it be judged?
options: Complete, because detail is the measure of documentation quality for any reader
Complete, because auditors read separate material in any case and need nothing here
Incomplete, because a document built for only one reader is incomplete even when detailed
Incomplete only if the deployment sits in a regulated industry with formal audits
questions.explanation: Serving one reader but not the others leaves the document incomplete regardless of detail. The returning architect and the auditor each need things this document lacks.
questions.mnemonic: Detail for one reader still leaves two readers stranded.

questions.stem: Why must a handoff document record rejected alternatives and the reason each was rejected?
options: So the auditor can see how many different options were considered during design
So the successor can tell which trade-off the design resolved and not reverse it wrongly
So the sales team can reuse the comparison in later proposals for other customers
So the document reaches the minimum length a compliance reviewer normally expects to see
questions.explanation: Rejected options explain why the design is shaped as it is; without them a successor cannot tell which trade-off a decision was resolving. The count of options is not what matters.
questions.mnemonic: The road not taken explains the road you're on.

questions.stem: For the compliance reviewer, which set of items must the document carry for each regulatory obligation?
options: The obligation, the satisfying control, its owner, and the evidence artifact showing it operates
The obligation, the vendor's compliance certificate, the project cost, and the go-live date
The control, the rejected alternative, the named tradeoff, and the planned reversal date
The obligation, the control, the monitoring dashboard, and the log of open assumptions
questions.explanation: The reviewer needs obligation, control, owner and evidence artifact, which is the control register carried forward into the living document. They do not accept a statement that a control exists.
questions.mnemonic: Obligation, control, owner, evidence: no proof, no pass.

questions.stem: A reviewer asks about request logging. The document says only, 'Logging is enabled on all calls.' What is the issue?
options: The statement is too short; it needs a diagram of the whole logging route
It names the control but gives no owner and no evidence artifact showing it operates
The statement should be removed because logging is merely a low-level technical detail
The statement is sufficient because reviewers accept the architect's attestation at face value
questions.explanation: A reviewer requires evidence, not assertions, so the control needs an owner and an evidence artifact. A diagram would still only show what exists, not that it operates.
questions.mnemonic: 'Enabled' is a claim; the artifact is the proof.

questions.stem: Which THREE features make a document navigable for an architect returning months later? Select THREE.
options: Decisions are dated so the sequence of choices can be followed later
Assumptions are explicitly labelled as assumptions, not embedded as settled facts
Open items have named owners and criteria for what counts as resolved
A short summary that leaves out rejected options to save the reader time
Technical vocabulary assumed to be familiar to the original design team members
questions.explanation: The returning architect needs dated decisions, assumptions labelled as such, and open items with owners and resolution criteria. Omitting rejected options or assuming shared vocabulary makes the document harder to use without a briefing.
questions.mnemonic: Dated, labelled, owned: a document that needs no briefing.

questions.stem: What is the practical test for whether architecture documentation is complete?
options: Whether it passes a length and formatting review by the compliance team
Whether the original architect agrees that it matches the design they built
Whether every component in the deployment appears somewhere in the architecture diagram
Whether a competent architect absent from the design sessions could make a safe change
questions.explanation: The test is whether a competent architect who was not in the room can make a safe change. A complete diagram or the original architect's approval does not show that.
questions.mnemonic: If a stranger can't change it safely, it isn't finished.

questions.stem: Which TWO checklist fields primarily serve the handoff recipient? Select TWO.
options: Evidence artifact showing the control is operating
Rejected alternatives and why each was set aside
Audit-ready status of the available evidence
Tradeoff named, with gains, costs and reversal implications
Decision date, serving only the compliance reviewer
questions.explanation: Rejected alternatives primarily serve the handoff recipient, and the named tradeoff serves the handoff recipient and the returning architect. Evidence artifact and audit-ready status primarily serve the compliance reviewer.
questions.mnemonic: Rejected options and named trade-offs are for the heir.

questions.stem: Which checklist field records whether the available evidence is current and sufficient for review?
options: Decision, recording the architectural choice made and its date
Audit-ready status, recording whether evidence is current and sufficient
Tradeoff named, recording gains, costs and reversal implications
Owner, recording who is responsible for the control going forward
questions.explanation: Audit-ready status captures whether the available evidence is current and sufficient, and it serves the compliance reviewer. Owner names who is responsible for the decision or control going forward.
questions.mnemonic: Audit-ready status: is the proof fresh enough to show?

questions.stem: Why is design rationale easy to leave out of architecture documentation?
options: Auditors prefer that rationale is kept out of the formal design record
Architecture diagrams already capture the reasoning behind every decision
Recording why, not just what, feels redundant to whoever lived the reasoning
Rationale belongs only in the customer outcome document written at close
questions.explanation: The discipline is recording why, not just what, and labelling assumptions as assumptions, which is easy to skip when the reasoning feels obvious to the person who lived it. A diagram records what was built; the why has to be written down separately.
questions.mnemonic: Obvious to you today, invisible to your successor tomorrow.

questions.stem: When should the decision, the rejected alternatives and the tradeoff each resolved be written down?
options: At design time, while the architect still holds the reasoning
At handoff, reconstructed from the project's email threads
When an auditor first requests evidence for a specific control
After the first production change shows which decisions mattered
questions.explanation: Write the rationale at design time, while you still hold the reasoning. Reconstructing it later from email threads, or failing to, costs a wrong reversal in production; if it is never written, it leaves with you.
questions.mnemonic: Write the why while you still know it, or it leaves with you.

questions.stem: In lifecycle terms, which mapping of artifacts to stages is correct?
options: Documentation is the discovery stage; the feedback loop is the design stage
Documentation is the handoff stage; the feedback loop is the monitoring-and-iteration stage
Documentation is the monitoring stage; the feedback loop is the handoff stage
Documentation is the design stage; the feedback loop is the discovery stage
questions.explanation: Documentation that survives your absence is the handoff stage, while the feedback loop keeps the live deployment healthy in the monitoring-and-iteration stage. The other mappings swap the stages.
questions.mnemonic: Write it for handoff; loop it for monitoring and iteration.

subjects.title: Entry-point selection in production and outcome documents
learn: In a live multi-platform deployment the route question becomes which entry point performs best across latency, cost and compliance, not just which survives the compliance pre-filter.

Cross-platform problems: model identifier strings differ, features can lag on cloud-provider routes, and Bedrock/Vertex need explicit regional configuration; defaulting to a global endpoint commonly breaks residency.
An entry-point-responsibility map says which entry point owns which task and why, preventing task creep; draw it before the first line of integration code.

Decision matrix: direct API by default unless procurement or residency points elsewhere; Bedrock or Vertex for AWS or GCP standardised partners; Foundry, verify residency and coverage per hosting form.

Outcome document: use case with scope boundary, metric before, metric after using the same definition, control making the comparison auditable, and measurement owner. Capture the before metric at the start.
traps: Global endpoint default: leaving a Bedrock or Vertex region unconfigured is the common way a residency requirement quietly breaks.
Assuming parity: model IDs differ across routes, and cloud-provider routes can lag direct API features.
Task creep: without a responsibility map, an entry point chosen for one task gradually takes on another.
Platform-name assumption: Foundry coverage depends on hosting form, so verify residency per route rather than from the name.
Easy metrics: technical metrics exported from the observability stack show the system runs, not what it changed; without a before metric on the business outcome there is no case for expansion.

questions.stem: How does the entry-point question change once a deployment is live across more than one platform?
options: It becomes only a procurement question settled by the customer's cloud contract alone
It no longer matters because the compliance pre-filter already decided the route
It becomes a question of which model name is cheapest on each platform
It becomes which route performs best across latency, cost and compliance in live use
questions.explanation: Earlier, route selection was a compliance pre-filter; with the full production picture the question is performance across latency, cost and compliance. Procurement is one input, not the whole question.
questions.mnemonic: Pre-filter picks who qualifies; production asks who performs.

questions.stem: A team ports a working integration from the direct API to a cloud-provider route and it fails to find the model. Which cross-platform issue is the most likely cause?
options: Model identifier strings differ across routes, so the identifier must be changed
Prompt caching is disabled on every cloud-provider route by default
The logging profile is identical across routes, which causes naming conflicts
The regional endpoint is always global on cloud-provider routes
questions.explanation: Model identifier strings differ across entry points, so a configuration that works on one route may not work on another. The other options are not stated cross-platform behaviours.
questions.mnemonic: Same model, different name: IDs change with the route.

questions.stem: Which TWO problems does a deployment spanning more than one entry point expose that a single-entry-point system does not? Select TWO.
options: Feature availability can lag on a cloud-provider route versus the direct API
Eval scores can no longer be compared between releases on different routes
Regional availability on Bedrock and Vertex requires explicit configuration
Every route must share one authentication method and one logging profile
Latency budgets no longer apply to deployments that span multiple routes
questions.explanation: Features can lag on cloud-provider routes, and Bedrock and Vertex regions need explicit configuration. Each route keeps its own authentication and logging profile, so a shared auth method is not required.
questions.mnemonic: IDs differ, features lag, regions need explicit setting.

questions.stem: Which common configuration pattern most often breaks a data-residency requirement on a Bedrock or Vertex deployment?
options: Using a different model identifier than the direct API
Defaulting to a global endpoint instead of explicitly configuring the region
Running two entry points inside the same workflow
Keeping the policy document in the prompt rather than in retrieval
questions.explanation: Regional availability needs explicit configuration, and defaulting to a global endpoint is the common residency breaker. Model identifiers affect compatibility rather than data location.
questions.mnemonic: Global by default means residency by accident.

questions.stem: A deployment passes testing, but a quarterly confirmation finds requests are being served outside the required region. Which cause should be investigated first?
options: A global endpoint default instead of an explicitly configured region
A model tier chosen above the pilot's needs, raising the monthly cost
An eval score drifting below the threshold set from the eval suite
A missing before metric in the outcome document written at close
questions.explanation: On Bedrock and Vertex, regional execution needs explicit configuration, and a global endpoint default is the usual way residency quietly breaks. The other options concern cost, quality and reporting.
questions.mnemonic: Residency drift? Check for a quiet global endpoint.

questions.stem: What does an entry-point-responsibility map record, and when should it exist?
options: Which entry point owns which task and why; before writing any integration code
Which entry point had the lowest cost; compiled after the first invoice arrives
Which team approved each route; recorded after the production cutover is done
Which entry point holds the logs; produced once an auditor asks for them
questions.explanation: The map says which entry point handles which task and why, and it should precede integration code because each boundary has its own auth, logging and failure profile. Writing it later invites undocumented routing.
questions.mnemonic: Map the owners before you write the integration.

questions.stem: Over a year, a cloud-provider entry point set up for one regulated workflow starts handling unrelated tasks nobody planned. Which missing artifact most directly allowed this?
options: A consumption forecast at expected production volume for each entry point
A governance table of production signals, triggers and owners for the loop
An entry-point-responsibility map stating which entry point owns which task and why
A measurement owner named in the outcome document after the engagement closes
questions.explanation: Task creep is the common multi-entry-point failure when routing logic was never documented; the responsibility map prevents it. The other artifacts address cost, drift and outcome measurement.
questions.mnemonic: Undocumented routing lets one entry point creep into another's job.

questions.stem: No procurement rule or residency requirement points elsewhere for a new deployment. Which entry point does the decision matrix suggest?
options: AWS Bedrock, because it is region-configurable for every deployment
GCP Vertex AI, because it fits any procurement path a partner has
The direct Anthropic API, the default unless procurement or residency says otherwise
Microsoft Foundry, because its platform name implies full residency coverage
questions.explanation: The direct API is the default, with newest features first and the fewest extra hops, unless a procurement or residency rule points elsewhere. Foundry coverage cannot be assumed from the platform name.
questions.mnemonic: Direct first, unless procurement or residency says otherwise.

questions.stem: A partner has standardised on AWS and needs in-region execution. Which entry point does the decision matrix favour, with what condition?
options: The direct API, with no regional configuration required
Microsoft Foundry, with residency assumed from the platform
GCP Vertex AI, with the region left at its default
AWS Bedrock, configured explicitly for the required region
questions.explanation: Bedrock fits AWS-centric procurement and region rules when configured explicitly, though features may lag the direct API. Vertex is the equivalent for GCP-standardised partners.
questions.mnemonic: AWS shop, in-region need: Bedrock, region set explicitly.

questions.stem: A partner requires Microsoft Foundry for procurement reasons. How should the architect handle data residency?
options: Assume the partner's Azure environment hosts inference for every model
Verify residency and coverage per hosting form, since hosted-on-Azure and hosted-on-Anthropic models differ
Treat residency as satisfied because Foundry is an Azure platform
Default to the global endpoint and confirm residency after cutover
questions.explanation: Foundry varies by hosting form: hosted-on-Azure models run inference in the partner's Azure environment, whereas hosted-on-Anthropic models route to Anthropic infrastructure. Residency must be verified per route, not assumed from the name.
questions.mnemonic: Foundry: check the hosting form, never the brand name.

questions.stem: Which THREE fields belong in a customer outcome document? Select THREE.
options: The use case with its scope boundary
Monthly request volume as the headline result
The business metric before deployment and after it, using the same definition
The control that makes the comparison auditable
Average latency as the proof of value
questions.explanation: The document records the use case with scope boundary, the before and after metric on the same definition, the control making the comparison auditable, and a measurement owner. Volume and latency are technical metrics, not business outcomes.
questions.mnemonic: Scope, before and after, control, owner: outcomes beat throughput.

questions.stem: Whom is a customer outcome document chiefly written for, and what must it let them do?
options: The on-call engineer, so incidents can be debugged after the engagement closes
The sponsor outside the build, to justify the deployment upward with business outcomes
The observability vendor, so that metric exports can be tuned to the use case
The original build team, as a change log of the releases made during delivery
questions.explanation: The outcome document makes the deployment's value understandable to people who were not on the build, chiefly the sponsor who must justify it upward. Technical metrics alone cannot do that; the before-and-after business outcomes can, and a metrics-only document cannot justify expansion.
questions.mnemonic: Written for the sponsor to take upstairs: business before-and-after, not uptime.

questions.stem: When should the architect capture the before metric for the outcome document?
options: At the start of the engagement, before the deployment changes anything
At project close, by estimating it back from the measured after result
At the first SLA review, pulled from the observability stack exports
Whenever the sponsor asks for funding to expand the deployment
questions.explanation: Without the before number there is no story, so it must be captured at the start. Reconstructing it afterwards leaves the comparison an assertion.
questions.mnemonic: No before, no story: baseline on day one.

questions.stem: Why does the outcome document include a control in place alongside the before and after metrics?
options: To assign an owner for the monitoring dashboards
To list the guardrails used in the prompts
To make the before-and-after comparison auditable rather than merely asserted
To record which entry point served each request
questions.explanation: Without a control, the after number is an assertion; the control lets a sponsor defend the comparison upward. The measurement owner is a separate field.
questions.mnemonic: Without a control, the after number is just a claim.

questions.stem: An engagement closes with an outcome document showing before and after metrics and an auditable control. Six months later nobody knows whether the gains have held. Which outcome-document field was missing?
options: Use case with scope boundary: what the deployment does and does not do
Metric after: the same business metric measured using the same definition
Measurement owner: who owns ongoing measurement after the engagement closes
Control in place: what makes the comparison auditable rather than asserted
questions.explanation: The measurement owner field names who is responsible for ongoing measurement once the engagement closes. The before and after metrics and the control were present, so the gap is that nobody owned keeping the measurement going.
questions.mnemonic: Engagement ends, measurement doesn't: name its owner.

questions.stem: Whom should the measurement owner field in a customer outcome document name?
options: The architect who built the deployment, since they defined the original metrics
The person or team responsible for ongoing measurement once the engagement closes
The CFO who approves expansion, since they consume the before-and-after figures
The observability vendor, since its stack exports the technical metrics automatically
questions.explanation: The field records who owns ongoing measurement after the engagement closes. The building architect leaves with the engagement, and the CFO consumes the result rather than measuring it.
questions.mnemonic: Owner outlasts the build team.
